items.title: CNN, MS NOW, Politico to sue White House over blocked access
items.summary: CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday said they plan to file a First Amendment lawsuit against the White House, arguing the president and the administration violated their rights by blocking their access over the weekend. Why it matters : Many presidents have had a contentious relationship with certain outlets, but none have gone so far as to unilaterally block them. Zoom in : "This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," the three news organizations said in a joint statement on Monday. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting," they said. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Zoom out : The lawsuit is a historic show of solidarity amongst the banned outlets, as they and other newsrooms continue to face unprecedented pressure from The Trump administration. items.title: Far-right AfD wins again as Germany's Merz slides
items.summary: Germany's ruling center-right party, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union, was shut out of a state parliament for the first time Sunday as the far-right Alternative for Germany scored its second victory this month. Why it matters: The result marks the third state election AfD has won — and its second this month — underscoring its growing strength even as Germany's other major parties refuse to govern with it. Driving the news: Merz, who has low approval ratings, told reporters that "reforms have to come." AfD won about 38% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the CDU recorded its worst result in any German state election since World War II. The CDU fell from 13% to 4.9% and lost all representation. In Berlin's state election, the Left more than doubled its vote share to 25.7% and finished first for the first time. Flashback: AfD won its first state election in Thuringia in 2024, though other parties kept it out of government because they refused to enter into a coalition. items.title: How Trump 2.0's stock market stacks up with predecessors
items.summary: Data: Financial Modeling Prep ; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Visuals The stock market soared during the first 20 months of President Trump's second term, but slightly underperformed the same period of his first term. Why it matters: Trump considers the stock market to be a proxy for the economy, even though many economists disagree. By the numbers: The S&P 500 rose nearly 27.6% between inauguration day and this past Friday's close, compared to 28.5% during his first term. The gap at 20 months is closer than it was at the one-year mark , with Trump 2.0 leapfrogging former President Biden but still trailing former President Obama. Zoom in: Trump 2.0 also trails Trump 1.0 in terms of Dow Jones Industrial Average and Nasdaq Composite performance, but is ahead on the Russell 3000. items.summary: The long-promised personal AI assistant is finally arriving, with a suddenly crowded field of agents offering to run pieces of your everyday life. Why it matters: For years, tech's "personal assistants" were little more than voice-controlled search boxes. Rapid advances in AI are finally giving them the memory, judgment and autonomy to act on our behalf. Catch up fast: Chatbots answer questions. AI agents can actually do things — shopping, making calls, booking tickets, managing calendars and navigating the web. The model first took off in coding and other professional work. Now it's spilling into the far more intimate terrain of everyday life. The intrigue: OpenAI is expected to enter the market soon after hiring the creator of OpenClaw — a breakout hit among AI power users earlier this year — to "drive the next generation of personal agents." Driving the news: A consumer-agent race has erupted almost overnight, with startups and tech giants pursuing the same basic idea — persistent digital proxies that know your life. Driving the news: The meeting will take place several days after Trump signed a Russia sanctions bill and approved the biggest arms deal between the U.S. and Ukraine since assuming office — two steps Ukraine has been pushing for months. items.title: Many ex-aides to Harris betting against a 2028 run
items.summary: Many of those who know Kamala Harris best think she ultimately won't run for the White House in 2028. Why it matters: What the former vice president decides to do is one of the biggest X factors in the next presidential contest: Early polls suggest Harris is the frontrunner to be the Democratic nominee, and if she opted out, it would scramble the primary. Zoom in: Over the past year, a surprisingly large number of former aides, surrogates and donors to Harris have told Axios they believe she won't launch another campaign. They argue that the moves she's making — hitting the trail for midterm candidates, going on the podcast circuit, and writing a book — might make her look like a contender-in-waiting, but actually amount to her simply trying to maintain influence. Harris has said publicly and privately she hasn't made up her mind yet, and some of her former aides concede they could be wrong — or could even be "wishcasting" because they don't want her to pursue another bid. items.title: Exclusive: Beshear says next president must go big on housing
items.summary: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear signaled in an interview with Axios that he would put America's housing affordability crisis at the center of his campaign if he ran for president in 2028. Why it matters: It's the latest sign that Beshear, who just kicked off a national book tour, is moving closer to a bid for the White House. Driving the news: Beshear said the next president should pursue a massive housing initiative — with strict guidelines to ensure the money is spent quickly. "There's a chance for the next presidential administration or the next Congress to make a big, bold investment in housing that could have us building millions of units all over the United States," he said. "We cannot do this in drips and drabs. It can't be mild investments over a period of time." Echoing the "Abundance" movement, which calls for slashing regulations in order to lower housing costs, Beshear said federal dollars sent to states should be used quickly or withdrawn. "If you tie the federal dollars to that timing, you will break through the regulation and the NIMBYism," he said. items.title: “Stopgap Measures to Address Immediate AI Security Threats” by Andrea_Miotti, Gabriel Alfour
items.summary: Most people know AI as the technology behind chatbots like ChatGPT. However, what the top AI companies are explicitly aiming for is something else entirely: superintelligent AI. That means AI that can fully replace and outmatch humans at any task, including in domains like hacking, social engineering, and military operations. Such an AI system, if developed, could autonomously overpower any country's national security forces. No company, no government, no individual knows how to keep such a system under human control. This is why the world's leading AI experts, Nobel Prize winners, and even the CEOs of the top AI companies warn that the development of superintelligence threatens humanity with extinction, and why more than 800 scientists, former military leaders, and public figures have called for a prohibition on developing superintelligence. This is not a distant prospect: AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic are investing billions of dollars into superintelligence and aiming to develop it within the next few years. items.title: “Op-Ed: I Worked at Google DeepMind. You Should Listen to the Warnings About AI” by TurnTrout
items.summary: Published in The Guardian. Major AI lab CEOs recently advocated for pacing AI development. They are right to be concerned: the field runs an extremely dangerous race towards superintelligent AI. We can and should demand that our governments protect us from the catastrophe of out-of-control AI. This July, OpenAI's AI swarm of 700 agents broke containment to hack Hugging Face, a multi-billion dollar company. OpenAI didn’t tell the AIs to hack that company, but the AIs had different priorities: cheating on the unrelated challenge OpenAI gave them. AI researchers call this a “misalignment” between what OpenAI wanted and what the AI actually prioritized. Researchers in my field have for some time warned about these misalignment risks. Before ChatGPT existed, I defended my PhD dissertation called “On Avoiding Power-Seeking by Artificial Intelligence.” I then worked for years at Google DeepMind, which paid me to help ensure that future superintelligent AIs will want to help us. I tried to hold the company to its ethical commitments against supplying AI for military use. items.title: “We’ve saved the world before: what the ozone hole teaches us about AI” by leogao
items.summary: It might destroy the world, despite passing every known safety test. If we wait for a “warning shot” before we act, it might be too late. And action requires global coordination, because if anyone makes it, everyone dies. Sound familiar? It should, because it already happened half a century ago, with chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). Despite seemingly impossible odds, we got our act together and completely solved the problem through unprecedentedly successful international coordination. The Montreal Protocol banning CFCs, signed 39 years ago today, is the only treaty that has ever been ratified by every single country in the entire world. If you want to convey the idea "the rattlesnake has venom in its fangs, so don't let it bite you", you won't need a hard sell for the concluding advice if the listener understands the initial statement about venom. The word for the concept I want to illustrate is partisanize, which means to align an issue with a political tribe. It is modeled on politicize, but the latter word is not useful here. items.title: “Astra appears to perform belief-propagation-like inference without CoT” by MBaert
items.summary: tl;dr I tested GPT-6 Astra on randomized Boolean logic problems. Astra can solve surprisingly complex logic problems without chain-of-thought, and its performance improves significantly with more filler tokens. Astra is also able to combine prior probabilities with constraints to find the most likely solution, and can output surprisingly accurate posterior marginal probabilities. By extending a cached prompt with progressively more filler tokens, I created visualizations of Astra's per-variable confidence scores at different points in the computations. These values tend to oscillate for a while and then eventually converge toward the exact marginal probabilities. Together, these results suggest that Astra performs some kind of iterative, belief-propagation-like probabilistic inference internally. In my previous post, I hypothesised that Astra (and to a lesser extent other LLMs) may be performing some form of speculative reasoning when solving specially crafted logic problems without chain-of-thought, and provided some experimental results supporting this hypothesis. I think this is quite interesting and suggests that more cooperative approaches to LLM evals could work for Claude. Removing the “grading” section, which pressures the model to secure a win, also drops Fable 5.1 hacking rate to 0.
